readerTitle: Being the only seller doesn't mean you can charge anything
caseNote: 가상 사례 (냉장 창고, 치과 소프트웨어 연동) + 실제 기업 (Xerox 복사기, 일반적 서술만)
insight: 독점력은 '경쟁자가 없다'는 사실이 아니라 '고객의 다음 선택지가 얼마나 비싼가'로 정해진다. 그리고 그 힘은 세게 쓸수록 빨리 줄어든다.
misconception: 유일한 판매자라면 원하는 만큼 가격을 올려도 고객은 따라올 수밖에 없다.

sources.text: FTC, In the Matter of Xerox Corporation, consent order (1975)
냉장 창고와 치과 소프트웨어 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Xerox 914(1959년 출시)와 보통 용지 복사 특허로 1960년대 사실상 유일한 공급자였다는 점, 1975년 FTC 동의명령으로 특허 라이선스가 의무화된 점을 1차 자료로 확인하세요. 시장 점유율 하락 수치는 자료마다 달라 카드에 숫자를 넣지 않았습니다.
Canon, Ricoh 등 일본 업체가 소형·저가 복사기로 진입했다는 서술이 정확한지 확인하세요. 카드에는 '일본 업체들(such as Canon and Ricoh)'로만 적었습니다.
냉장 창고 사례: 40% 인상, 200km 거리, 트럭 운송비 등은 모두 가상입니다. 구체적 계산은 넣지 않았습니다.
경쟁법 관련 문장은 일반적 언급에 그치며 특정 국가의 법률 조언이 아님을 확인하세요.

cards.title: Being the only seller doesn't mean you can charge anything
body: A family firm owns the only cold-storage warehouse within 200 km of a fruit-growing valley. Every harvest, growers have nowhere else to keep their apples cold.
One year the owner raised prices 40%. Two seasons later, the warehouse was half empty.

image.label: A lone warehouse in a valley of orchards, with trucks driving away
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 과수원 계곡 한가운데 냉장 창고 한 동. 사과 상자를 실은 냉장 트럭들이 창고를 지나쳐 계곡 밖으로 빠져나가는 모습. 실제 회사 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: You're the only warehouse in the valley.
body: Demand is steady and your costs went up a little. Growers grumble about prices but have always paid.
How do you set next season's price?

options.text: Raise it sharply. They have no other warehouse nearby.
options.feedback: You gain a big margin this season, but you're betting growers have no other option at all. Expensive enough prices create options.

options.text: Raise it modestly and lock growers into five-year contracts
options.feedback: Contracts buy time and protect revenue. But if your price is far above their alternatives, they'll leave the day the contract ends.

options.text: First work out what their next-best option costs, then price below it
options.feedback: Your real ceiling is the cost of the alternative, not your lack of rivals. Staying under it keeps customers from looking for one.

cards.title: The "no choice" customers found choices.
body: At the old price, trucking fruit to a warehouse three hours away made no sense. At 40% more, it did. Several growers rented refrigerated trucks and shipped out.
Others joined a co-op and started building their own cooled storage shed. A logistics company noticed the gap and began planning a second warehouse.
The owner had been the only seller. That turned out to be different from having **no competition**.

cards.title: Monopoly power
body: **Monopoly power** is the ability to raise prices above what competition would allow without losing too many customers.

It isn't the same as being the only seller. It depends on what customers can do instead: a substitute product, a farther supplier, doing it themselves, or simply buying less. The cheaper those options, the less power you have.

image.label: A price bar rising until it crosses the cost of the next-best option
image.brief: 막대 그래프 인포그래픽. 창고 가격 막대가 점점 올라가다가 점선으로 표시된 "Next-best option: truck to another warehouse" 높이를 넘는 순간 고객 아이콘들이 화살표를 따라 빠져나감. 점선을 '진짜 가격 상한'으로 강조.

cards.title: Xerox had the patents. Rivals found a way in.
body: In the 1960s, Xerox was close to the only maker of plain-paper office copiers, thanks to its patents. It earned large profits leasing big, expensive machines.

Those high prices were a signal. In 1975, a settlement with the US Federal Trade Commission required Xerox to license its copier patents. Japanese makers, such as Canon and Ricoh, moved in with smaller, cheaper machines that many offices preferred. Xerox's share fell sharply.
Strong profits showed rivals exactly where the money was.

image.label: One giant copier facing a line of small, cheap copiers
image.brief: 레트로 사무실 배경. 왼쪽에 거대한 복사기 한 대, 오른쪽에 작은 복사기들이 줄지어 다가오는 장면. 실제 브랜드 로고와 제품 디자인은 쓰지 말 것.

cards.title: Four things keep customers from leaving.
body: Monopoly power lasts only while something makes the alternatives costly:
list: **No close substitutes:** nothing else does the job nearly as well
**Barriers to entry:** licenses, scarce locations or huge setup costs
**Switching costs:** moving data, retraining staff, breaking contracts
**Hard to do yourself:** customers can't easily build their own
cards.callout: Push prices up hard, and you give customers a reason to knock each of these down.

cards.title: Real monopoly power does exist.
body: This isn't a promise that every monopoly fades. A water utility, a key patent or a network everyone already uses can hold strong power for decades.

And using power hard has other costs. Customers remember being squeezed. Many countries also have competition laws that limit how dominant firms can behave, so check local rules with an expert before relying on a dominant position.

cards.title: Now it's software.
body: Your small software company makes the only tool that connects a popular dental-records system to online booking. About 2,000 clinics pay you $40 a month.
Your team wants to triple the price. What do you do?

options.text: Triple it. No one else offers this connection.
options.feedback: Revenue jumps at first. But $120 a month gives the records company, or a rival developer, a strong reason to build the connection and take your users.

options.text: Keep $40 and add features that make switching harder
options.feedback: Higher switching costs do protect you. But leaving the price untouched may undercharge clinics who get far more value than $40.

options.text: Raise prices moderately, tied to new value, and watch for anyone building a rival tool
options.feedback: You earn more while staying below the point where building an alternative pays. You trade some short-term profit for a position that lasts.

cards.title: Your pricing power ends where your customers' next option begins.
body: Being the only seller tells you little. What matters is how costly it is for customers to switch, substitute or build their own, and how fast that changes when you raise prices.
**Try it today:** for your main product, write down what a customer would do if you doubled the price. Estimate what that option costs them.
